consensus_summary: The blind consensus treats 'shadow' as a polyvalent biblical image with two competing primary senses: (1) divine protection/refuge under God's covering (Ps 91:1; 17:8; 36:7) and (2) typological foreshadowing — Old Testament laws, festivals, priesthood, and sanctuary as a 'shadow' of the substance found in Christ (Col 2:16-17; Heb 8:5; 10:1). Secondary parallel senses include the transience of human life, the 'shadow of death' (deep darkness/mortal danger), mutability (James 1:17), and conveyed healing power (Acts 5:15). All four responses list protection, typology, transience, and death as coordinate senses.
book_summary: The book defines shadow as an object or activity shaped like the substance that casts it, marking the reach and boundary of that substance's covering. It identifies the appointed times and holy assemblies (Lev 23 feasts) as the Shadow of Christ's substance, and treats 'Shadow of Death' not as another sense of shadow but as the opposite of this shadow — a rival covering.
consensus_core_identification: Shadow = context-dependent symbol whose leading senses are (a) protective covering under God and (b) typological prefiguration of Christ's reality, with transience and the shadow of death as coordinate additional senses.
book_core_identification: Shadow = a shape cast by a substance that marks the extent of that substance's covering; specifically, the appointed times/holy convocations are Christ's shadow (his covering's reach), with the Shadow of Death as the opposing covering.
boundary_disagreement: The book fuses two senses the consensus keeps separate — typological foreshadowing (Col 2:17; Heb 8:5; 10:1) and protective covering (Ps 91:1; Num 14:9) — into one unified definition: the shadow both prefigures the substance and marks the boundary of its protection. It narrows the typological referent specifically to the appointed times and holy assemblies (Lev 23). It also reclassifies the 'shadow of death,' which the consensus lists as simply another sense of the same word, as a structural opposite of Christ's shadow rather than a coordinate meaning; and it silently drops the transience and mutability senses (Job 8:9; James 1:17) from the definition.
rationale: The book's central referent remains within the consensus map: the shadow/substance typology of Colossians and Hebrews, which every response lists as primary or dominant, combined with the protective-covering sense that Responses A and B rank first. There is no replacement of referent, so this is not DIVERGENT. But the book materially reworks the boundaries: it merges protection and typology into a single mechanism ('marking the reach and boundary of that substance's covering'), fixes the typological extension on the appointed times/feasts specifically, converts 'Shadow of Death' from a parallel sense into a defined opposite, and excludes the transience sense entirely. These are real extensional changes, not mere wording, so REFINED with PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION fits.
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH: the book's core is simply the Col 2:17/Heb 10:1 shadow-substance typology that Responses C and D already make primary, and the 'covering' language is just an elaboration consistent with Ps 91:1, which Responses A and B also cite; the omission of other senses could be treated as immaterial compression in a short glossary entry. Against this, the explicit unification of protection with typology, the restriction to appointed times, and the formal opposition to 'Shadow of Death' go beyond wording and change which cases count as 'shadow' in the book's system.
